Yes, such a meromorphic function exists. Here is an explicit construction and verification.

**Construction.** Let
$$f(z) = \frac{z(z-1)}{z-\tfrac12}.$$
This is a rational function, hence meromorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$, with a single (simple) pole at $z=\tfrac12$.

**Zeros.** The zeros of $f$ are exactly the zeros of the numerator $z(z-1)$ that are not cancelled by the denominator, namely $z_1=0$ and $z_2=1$. Since $\deg(\text{num})-\deg(\text{den})=1$, we have $f(z)\sim z$ as $z\to\infty$, so $\infty$ is a simple pole, not a zero. Thus $f$ has **exactly two zeros**, $0$ and $1$, both simple.

**Derivatives at the zeros.** Write $f(z)=N(z)/D(z)$ with $N(z)=z(z-1)$, $D(z)=z-\tfrac12$. Then
$$f'(z)=\frac{N'(z)D(z)-N(z)D'(z)}{D(z)^2}=\frac{(2z-1)(z-\tfrac12)-z(z-1)}{(z-\tfrac12)^2}.$$

At $z_1=0$:
$$f'(0)=\frac{(-1)(-\tfrac12)-0}{(-\tfrac12)^2}=\frac{\tfrac12}{\tfrac14}=2.$$

At $z_2=1$:
$$f'(1)=\frac{(1)(\tfrac12)-0}{(\tfrac12)^2}=\frac{\tfrac12}{\tfrac14}=2.$$

Both $f'(0)=2$ and $f'(1)=2$ are real and strictly positive, so in particular $\operatorname{Re} f'(z_1)>0$ and $\operatorname{Re} f'(z_2)>0$.

**Conclusion.** The function $f(z)=\dfrac{z(z-1)}{z-1/2}$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$, has exactly two zeros $z_1=0$ and $z_2=1$, and satisfies $\operatorname{Re} f'(z_1)=\operatorname{Re} f'(z_2)=2>0$. Therefore such a meromorphic function exists.
